title: Asking the right questions about the psychology of human inquiry: Nine open challenges
extended_summary:
This paper is a critical theoretical review of the Optimal Experiment Design (OED) hypothesis as a framework for explaining human inquiry. The authors ask whether people really behave like intuitive scientists when they ask questions, explore the world, and choose interventions to reduce uncertainty. Rather than presenting a new educational intervention or empirical study, the paper examines how OED has been used across psychology to model inquiry behaviors such as question asking, exploratory play, hypothesis testing, causal intervention, and visual search.

The article reviews core OED assumptions, including explicit hypothesis spaces, candidate queries, and expected information gain, and shows how these assumptions have been used to model behavior in tasks such as the Wason selection task, causal-learning interventions, and children’s exploratory play. The paper also highlights where OED models succeed and where they are limited, arguing that the framework often depends on strong auxiliary assumptions and can be too narrow to capture inquiry that is based on vague goals, single hypotheses, or no explicit hypotheses at all.

The main contribution is a research agenda: nine open questions about how people construct hypotheses, generate candidate queries, decide what counts as a good answer, and how cognitive constraints shape inquiry. The paper concludes that OED remains a useful but incomplete account of human inquiry, and that future work should better integrate computational, algorithmic, and developmental explanations rather than treating inquiry as purely optimal information gain.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical critical review, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not evaluate a baseline/counterfactual condition with primary data, so there is no research design to rate under an evidence hierarchy.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured educational impact; it offers conceptual guidance about inquiry models rather than evidence of effects on learning, teaching, or operational outcomes.
